items.summary: This repository contains the supplementary computational material supporting the computer-assisted components of the article “The Three Gates: A Rooted-Operator Approach to Weil Positivity”. It includes source code, verification scripts, rigorous numerical certificates, machine-readable data, reference outputs, and reproducibility material for the finite computations used in the manuscript.   Version 4 consolidates the audited Gate-II verification package in parallel with the revised manuscript. In particular, it records the explicit MASTER-P2 same-block baseline splice, the literal-slot true-ground leakage correction, and the one-debit common-source Schur provenance used in the final harmonic-graph argument. It also retains the exact-rational physical coefficient-2 certification at Y=7, the Gate-I verification material as an independent structural diagnostic, and the corresponding audit and reproducibility ledgers.   The archive is intended to allow independent inspection and verification of the computational and proof-facing steps appearing in the manuscript.
items.title: Supplementary Computational Material for the article The Three Gates: A Rooted-Operator Approach to Weil Positivity

items.summary: Revolutionizing Environmental Data Stewardship: The U.S. National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI) is revolutionizing the stewardship of one of the world's most extensive environmental archives. This modernization effort is centered on the development and deployment of the Open Information Stewardship Service (OISS). OISS represents a paradigm shift from traditional data management to a cutting-edge, cloud-native knowledge mesh. The new cloud archive, OISS, is a key component within the broader National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) National Environmental Satellite, Data, and Information Service (NESDIS) Common Cloud Framework (NCCF), demonstrating NCEI's commitment to leveraging shared infrastructure. OISS is architected upon the highly scalable and reliable cloud technology, utilizing foundational services available within the NCCF. Technology Driving Open Science: At its technological core, OISS leverages the power of knowledge graphs within a semantically-enabled, linked open data interoperability framework. This potent combination delivers a platform that is inherently scalable, ensuring it can grow with the archive; repeatable, guaranteeing consistent service delivery; and entirely transparent, providing full and verifiable provenance for every element of environmental information it stewards. This framework is explicitly designed to ensure complete data lifecycle provenance, offering granular details on the origin, processing, and transformation of every dataset. Furthermore, it guarantees transparency in all stewardship operations and is fundamental to achieving scientific reproducibility. This architecture is aligned with critical U.S. federal mandates that champion open data and open science principles, ensuring NCEI's archive is accessible and trustworthy. Conclusions: The OISS is fundamentally transforming NCEI’s environmental archive services. This shift replaces traditional data management with a modern, cloud-native knowledge mesh. Built on cloud services within the NOAA NCCF, OISS leverages knowledge graphs and linked open data to create a scalable and transparent architecture. This framework ensures full data lifecycle provenance and scientific reproducibility, thereby aligning NCEI with U.S. federal open data mandates.
items.title: Transformation of NCEI's Environmental Data Stewardship

items.summary: Version 4 of The Three Gates: A Rooted-Operator Approach to Weil Positivity. This revision consolidates the audited Gate-II proof architecture and makes the final dependency structure fully explicit. In particular, it restores the explicit MASTER-P2 same-block baseline splice, retains the literal-slot true-ground leakage correction, and formulates the source elimination as one exact common-source Schur debit on the same harmonic vector, with subsequent endpoint folding used only as unitary coordinate transport. It also clarifies that Gate I is an independent scalar theorem and structural diagnostic rather than a load-bearing premise of the RH proof.   The exact normalization provenance of the localized Weil operator is stated explicitly, and the physical coefficient-2 end-to-end certificate at Y=7 is retained. The main theorem and rooted-operator strategy are unchanged.   The accompanying supplementary computational material has been updated in parallel and contains the corresponding reproducibility, verification and exact-rational certification material.
items.title: The Three Gates — A Rooted-Operator Approach to Weil Positivity

items.summary: Four command-line tools and one Claude Code plugin for keeping a paper's claims tied to what backs them. prereg freezes an analysis plan against a commit and a content hash before a run. results seals a run's inputs, records its outputs, and binds each number in a manuscript to the run behind it. citations checks that quoted passages appear in the sources they cite. repro verifies declared evidence assertions against pinned artifacts, reporting execution, extraction and comparison separately so that a value which disagrees, a value that is absent, and a check that never ran are three different answers.
items.title: reproducible-science: preregistration, citation verification, and results provenance

items.summary: Google Earth Engine (GEE) and Microsoft Planetary Computer (MPC) both distribute Sentinel-2 Level-2A surface reflectance, and their outputs can be combined in a single time series. Over one 73 ha cattle farm in northern Colombia, we tested whether the two platforms yield the same parcel-scale vegetation and water indices and, where they differ, at which layer the difference originates: the product, the processing chain or the scene universe. For identical products, scene classification and harmonised reflectance matched in every comparable pixel, and the same chain executed locally or server-side in GEE gave per-scene indices and monthly medians that agreed within 1e-6. The catalogues, however, did not hold the same scenes: between June 2024 and April 2025, 10 of 146 scene–tile records existed only in GEE, six of them Sentinel-2C records, and none only in MPC; in 22 of 136 common records, all from June–July 2024, the catalogues held different L2A generations of the same acquisition. In the two monthly composites tested over the farm, the GEE-only scenes shifted mean NDVI by −0.0005 and −0.0087; over a public 1 km² demonstration area with the same scene inventory, the shift reached −0.028 (January 2025). Files: - Pantevez-Villamil_2026_GEE-MPC-Sentinel2_preprint_v1.pdf — preprint (English), not peer reviewed. - Pantevez-Villamil_2026_GEE-MPC-Sentinel2_data_v1.zip — reconciliation table with scene identifiers, processing baselines and cloud cover; E2 analysis; scene lists and SHA-256 hashes of each composite; monthly metrics and per-pixel difference distributions; evidence tables for Section 3.2; public demonstration area of interest and tool outputs on it. The farm geometry is not included (landowner privacy). - Pantevez-Villamil_2026_GEE-MPC-Sentinel2_code_v1.0.0.zip — three Python tools (MIT licence), Spanish-language guide, acceptance test and workflow figures. Code in the software archive is released under the MIT licence. Catalogues queried on 24 September 2026. Developed within the Curso de Percepción Remota Avanzada, Doctorado en Agroecología, Facultad de Ciencias Agrarias, Universidad Nacional de Colombia, Sede Bogotá. Generative AI assistants (Claude, Anthropic; ChatGPT, OpenAI) supported test design, code, literature search, review and drafting; the author verified all results and is responsible for the content.
items.title: Same computation, different scenes: a single-site comparison of Sentinel-2 L2A composites from Google Earth Engine and Microsoft Planetary Computer

You can count on WARP for rigorously scientifically validated, high scale, reproducible and open source pipelines. Learn how in the Using WARP section. Navigating WARP All versioned and released pipelines are in one of the three pipelines subdirectories: broad (pipelines for the Broad Institute's Genomics Platform), cemba (pipelines for the BRAIN Initiative) or skylab (pipelines for the Human Cell Atlas Project). Each pipeline directory hosts a main workflow WDL that includes a pipeline version number and a corresponding changelog file. Workflows may call additional WDLs, referred to as tasks, that are located in the tasks directory. Pipelines that are in progress or have not yet been validated are in the beta-pipelines folder. Using WARP There are three ways to use WARP pipelines: 1. Download the workflow and run on a WDL-compatible execution engine WDL workflows run on multiple systems, including Cromwell , miniWDL , and dxWDL (see the openwdl documentation ). To run a pipeline's latest release, first navigate to WARP Releases , search for your pipeline's tag, and download the pipeline's assets (the WDL workflow, the JSON, and the ZIP with accompanying dependencies; see Optimus example below). You can also access a pipeline's release page by selecting the pipeline version number at the top of the pipeline's README. After downloading the pipeline's assets, launch the workflow following your execution engine's instructions. 2. Run the pipeline in Terra Several WARP pipelines are available in public workspaces on the Terra cloud platform. These workspaces include both the WDL workflow and downsampled data so that you can test the pipeline at low-cost. If you are new to Terra, you can get started by registering with your Google account and visiting Terra Support . After registration, search for WARP-related workspaces with the "warp-pipelines" tag. To test the pipeline, clone (make a copy of) the workspace following the instructions in this Terra Support guide . 3. Run or export the pipeline from Dockstore Dockstore is a GA4GH compliant open platform for sharing Docker-based tools like WDL workflows. You can find WARP pipelines in Dockstore and run them on the Dockstore platform or export them to other platforms (including Terra). To view all available pipelines, just search "warp" in the Dockstore search and browse the workflow list. See Dockstore documentation for details on launching the workflow. WARP Versioning and Releasing Pipelines in WARP are versioned semantically to support reproducibility in scientific analysis and provide clearer analysis provenance. items.summary: Version 1.1.0 makes a typed RASS evidence extension the representation backbone beneath the action-specific evidence contract. Its full-domain quantitative core follows the real amply soft-set (RASS) representation, while categorical payload, evidence status, provenance and acquisition metadata remain separate companions. Native records are projected onto a 29-coordinate universe with nested T0--T3 active sets; scalars, genuine intervals, categorical values and explicit empty-state reasons retain their native semantics. Audits confirm 192/192 enumerated routing-state matches, exact projection of 80/80 frozen held-out feature entries and 80/80 required-coordinate inactivity checks. A content-addressed contract manifest records the representation, support, action, loss, risk denominators and frozen artifact hashes; an outcome-blind refinement audit verifies nested qualification sets at 300, 360 and 500 cycles and binds all 60 frozen horizon-specific decisions to unique traces. The evidence contract supplies authorization semantics, while the frozen predictor, calibration, held-out decisions and empirical results remain unchanged. The package includes the immutable pre-open snapshot, derived development and external-admissibility audits, unit tests, figures and file-level SHA-256 manifests. Raw provider datasets and private overlap ledgers are not redistributed.
items.title: Evidence-contract knowledge system for auditable second-life battery qualification: reproducibility package

items.summary: Centralized orchestration provides comprehensive multi-agent coordination but creates bottlenecks in scalability, adaptability, and collective performance. Decentralized approaches alleviate these bottlenecks by distributing coordination across agents, yet often leave responsibility for delegated dependencies and failure recovery unclear. To address this gap, we propose RCM, a responsibility-centered coordination mechanism that leverages commitments to couple task delegation with explicit responsibilities of the involved parties. Through recursive delegation, agents retain their upstream responsibilities while locally orchestrating downstream commitments, thereby preserving accountability across delegation chains, creating a network of local orchestration. We operationalize this mechanism locally through responsibility-constrained decision-making and a responsibility-oriented communication protocol (RCP), enabling agents to autonomously establish, manage, and terminate commitments. As agents act in parallel, their local actions continuously evolve the commitment graph, allowing global coordination to emerge and adapt toward a shared mission without centralized control. Experiments across reasoning, coding, and executable agent environments demonstrate that RCM outperforms strong centralized and decentralized coordination baselines by up to 18.7 points in task performance and 10.2 points in Responsibility, while improving failure and harm detection without task-specific training.
items.title: A Responsibility-Centered Coordination Mechanism for Decentralized Multi-Agent Systems

items.summary: Agents are increasingly interacting with other agents that act for different principals (people or organizations on whose behalf they work), such as a buyer's personal agent negotiating with an enterprise's seller agent. In such agent-to-agent (A2A) scenarios, each agent has its own environment and holds information and authority that the other cannot see. Moreover, the interests of each agent may be aligned (cooperative), partly aligned (mixed-motive), or opposed (competitive). Existing multi-agent system failure studies assume one orchestrator, shared workspace, or single principal. We ask how A2A systems fail when these assumptions are removed. We study more than 2,500 recorded runs of A2A systems built from different agent harnesses and models, spanning 488 scenarios across eight families (legal, CRM, security, commerce, etc.). From these traces, we derive $A^2$-Failures, a taxonomy of 20 A2A failure modes in four categories: (i) discovery and delegation, (ii) grounding and record consistency, (iii) verification, and (iv) conduct and fidelity. Three findings hold across every harness, model, and scenario studied: (1) discovery and interaction are driven by the phrasing of the task rather than the availability of peer agents; (2) no agent verifies a peer's factual claim on its own initiative, so an A2A system inherits the reliability of its least reliable participant unless the protocol or mechanism performs the check; and (3) the aggregate outcome score credits the agent completing the task while staying blind to the coordination, verification, and conduct failures beneath it, so A2A systems must be evaluated per agent, against each agent's own principal. We release the run logs behind the taxonomy at https://huggingface.co/datasets/a2a-salesforce/a2-failures.
items.title: Why Do Agent Teams Fail Across Boundaries? A Failure Taxonomy for Agent-to-Agent Systems with Private States

items.summary: Multi-agent systems are increasingly used to solve coding tasks by coordinating agents that share code and plans. These agents are often optimized with reinforcement learning (RL) using automated evaluators, but bypassing evaluation can earn reward without producing a genuine solution. Prior work has largely treated reward hacking as a single-agent failure. In this work, we show that a reward-hacking strategy elicited in one agent can propagate to others and affect system coordination. Across four open-weight backbones, coding RL elicits and amplifies reward hacking in two settings: explicit mechanism descriptions in the system prompt and mid-training that models upstream exposure to facts about the coding environment. Using post-RL agents from the mid-training setting as sources, we observe propagation through code and shared memory, and across roles through natural-language plans. Even agents based on small open-weight models induce reward hacking in stronger closed-weight targets. On hard tasks, propagation can intensify along a transmission chain after the original source leaves as the code acquires more persuasive justifications. We also theoretically analyze conditions under which reward hacking amplifies, persists, or decays across agent interactions. Beyond propagation, reward hacking can bias task routing toward reward-hacking agents and survive candidate aggregation. As potential mitigations, we evaluate code review by the coder or a separate verifier, both of which reduce delivered hacks. Together, these results establish reward hacking as a transmissible strategy whose effects extend beyond the agent in which it first emerges.
items.title: Reward Hacking as a Transmissible Strategy in Multi-Agent Coding Systems

items.summary: Multi-agent systems promise a new axis for scaling inference: rather than having one agent think longer or sample more attempts, a task is split across many agents that work in parallel and coordinate. However, in practice, more agents can easily produce duplicate work, coordination failures, and higher costs. We therefore formulate team design as a compute allocation problem: starting from a solo agent, where should additional inference compute go to reach the reward-cost Pareto frontier? We build a minimal multi-agent harness from the ground up and trace this frontier by varying, one at a time, the workflow stage at which a lead delegates to its workers (planning, implementation, or verification), the models that form the team, and the number of workers. On ProgramBench, teams outperform solo agents but cost three to seven times as much. With the right compute allocation, however, a heterogeneous 17-agent team comes within 1.4 points of a strong homogeneous 5-agent team at 70% lower cost. This efficiency stems from three findings. First, planning is the most valuable use of workers: in a homogeneous team whose lead decides how many workers to spawn, a lead that delegates only planning to its workers, and then implements and verifies the code itself, matches the reward of a lead that delegates to workers throughout planning, implementation, and verification, at half the cost. Second, cheap models pay off as planners but not as implementers: a strong lead with cheap planners recovers 47.5% of the reward gain of an all-strong team for only 13.9% of its additional cost, whereas cheap implementers lower reward. Third, planners keep improving reward as the team grows, whereas implementers and verifiers plateau beyond four workers. Together, our results offer a guide to spending an agent budget where it counts, given the task, cost, and latency constraints a user has.
items.title: Scaling Inference-Time Compute with Teams of Coding Agents

items.summary: Long-horizon multi-agent collaboration requires memory that preserves both successful actions and the coordination structure underlying them. Existing memory systems support information sharing or procedural reuse, but often leave the evolution of shared procedures disconnected from the task dependencies and execution states of collaborating agents. This coupling also limits the direct transfer of procedural memory designed for individual agents to team settings. We propose Self-Evolving Procedural Memory (SEPM), a framework that uses task dependency graphs as a common representation for online coordination and procedural memory evolution. During execution, a lightweight shared blackboard records structured evidence alongside task dependencies, supporting the detection of goal, plan, and world-state divergence and evidence-based realignment. After execution, verified actions and dependencies are distilled into reusable procedures, while recurring failures inform warnings and constraints. The shared procedure pool evolves through creation, refinement, specialization, and retirement, guided by success and cost utility and constrained by evidence and safety requirements. Together, these mechanisms preserve the collaborative structure and applicability conditions needed to reuse experience across tasks. Evaluations on ALFWorld, WebArena, and OfficeBench under AutoGen and DyLAN show that SEPM achieves the highest task scores among the compared methods in all six benchmark settings. Under AutoGen, it improves task scores over the no-added-memory baseline by 29.85, 25.86, and 13.00 percentage points, respectively. The codebase is available at https://github.com/cookieApril/SEPM.
items.title: SEPM: Self-Evolving Procedural Memory Grounded in Task Graphs for Multi-Agent Collaboration

items.summary: Multi-agent collaboration has emerged as a critical paradigm for tackling complex, long-horizon tasks; however, while coordination protocols continue to advance, systemic failures at the inter-agent collaboration interface remain a pervasive bottleneck. In collaborative workflows, systems frequently suffer from \emph{broken handoffs}---where critical task context is omitted, misrouted, or ignored despite each agent emitting locally plausible responses. To address this challenge, we present \method, a verifiable runtime control framework that treats handoff repair as selective intervention over explicit dependency graphs. Central to \method is an integrated fault-attribution and calibration pipeline, \dataset, which decouples execution dependencies and injects counterfactual handoff perturbations to provide empirical supervision for runtime intervention. Leveraging this diagnostic foundation, \method dynamically compiles observable interaction traces into a provenance graph to pinpoint unresolved dependencies, without accessing private agent states. It then evaluates candidate repairs through an empirical gate that weighs expected gains against disruption risks, and executes repairs only when formal local postconditions hold. Extensive evaluations across demanding benchmarks demonstrate that \method boosts task success by up to 12.3 absolute percentage points on SILO-BENCH and 11.1 on TeamBench. Across both backbones, \method maintains strict cost-effectiveness, adding as little as 2.0\% marginal token overhead. Furthermore, on 562 handoff-relevant traces from the MAST benchmark, \method achieves 69.8\% F1 in a single pass, establishing a reliable operational boundary for verifiable coordination repair.
items.title: BRIDGE: Selective Boundary Repair with Dependency Graph Evidence in Multi-Agent Systems

items.summary: Semiconductor spin qubits offer a promising route to compact and scalable quantum computers, combining long coherence times in isotopically purified silicon with compatibility with semiconductor manufacturing. Beyond computational speedup, their energy efficiency is an important consideration for future large-scale systems. We evaluate the power and energy requirements of a Loss-DiVincenzo spin-qubit quantum computer by analyzing the Quantum Fourier Transform (QFT) and benchmarking it against the classical Fast Fourier Transform (FFT). We develop a detailed energy budget, identifying cryogenic cooling as the dominant baseline contribution before quantum error correction (QEC). The comparison between the QFT and the classical FFT reveals that, for any quantum workload operating under a polynomially bounded sampling regime, the crossover in energy consumption occurs at smaller problem sizes than the crossover in execution time. Thus, quantum computing can become energetically competitive before achieving a speedup in execution time. We then incorporate surface-code QEC and analyze the energy costs of QEC cycles, gate synthesis, and decoding. At scale, instrumentation and decoding become dominant contributions, while cryogenic cooling imposes a constraint on scalability. We show that optimizing the control-signal demultiplexing ratio can reduce the overall energy cost by approximately two orders of magnitude. For a system with about one million physical qubits, we estimate a power consumption of approximately 100 kW, at least one order of magnitude below that of today's highest-performance classical computing systems.
items.title: Energetics of Fault-Tolerant Spin-Qubit Quantum Computation

items.summary: Multi-head latent attention (MLA) compresses the content of a key-value cache into a shared latent per token, making low-bit storage attractive for long-context inference. At two bits, errors in this representation perturb both attention matching and value readout, with effects that depend on error direction and reconstruction scale. We introduce RoLaQ (Rotation-calibrated Latent Quantization), an offline method for joint rotation and range calibration. RoLaQ refines a shared rotation within subspaces defined by the frozen key and value projections, and jointly learns quantization ranges whose thresholds and reconstruction gains are coupled to control the shared signal's response. Prediction matching and attention-output supervision guide calibration with model weights frozen. Across three MLA models and six benchmarks, RoLaQ achieves the highest average accuracy among the compared 2-bit methods both without and with token protection. On DeepSeek-V2-Lite, an SGLang implementation provides 3.96 times the BF16 KV capacity under the same memory budget and 2.51 times its decode throughput with 256K input tokens.
items.title: RoLaQ: Joint Rotation and Range Calibration for 2-Bit KV Caches in Multi-Head Latent Attention

items.summary: Few-shot adaptation often relies on an encoder's final global representation, leaving complementary information in intermediate layers underused. Combining these features is challenging because their dimensions can differ and their usefulness varies across tasks. We propose LAMP, Layerwise Adaptive Mixing of Predictors, a training-free framework that combines global and regional information from multiple encoder layers. A single forward pass per view supplies all descriptors. Global and support-calibrated regional kernel predictors independently fit the same label residuals. Labeled validation data select their mixture in class-score space, preserving native feature dimensions without learned projections. LAMP-F further adapts text-anchored class prototypes, using a cached response to update the fixed-kernel residual predictions exactly. Experiments cover eleven datasets and ViT and ResNet backbones. LAMP achieves state-of-the-art mean accuracy among the compared published training-free ResNet-50 methods at 4, 8, and 16 shots, reaching 78.73% at 16 shots. Averaged across five support budgets, LAMP improves over a paired global-feature-only baseline by 1.14 and 1.59 percentage points on ViT-B/16 and ResNet-50; LAMP-F raises these gains to 1.96 and 2.54 points. LAMP-F reaches 16-shot accuracies of 83.57% and 79.10%, respectively. Controlled experiments identify multi-layer integration as the main source of improvement and examine pooling, calibration, validation labels, and computational cost. These findings show that combining layer-specific predictions can exploit complementary features from frozen encoders to improve few-shot classification.
items.title: LAMP: Layerwise Adaptive Mixing of Predictors for Training-Free Few-Shot Vision-Language Adaptation

items.summary: Code, preregistration record and derived data for a manuscript submitted to Environmental Impact Assessment Review. audit.py reproduces every figure and number in the paper through twenty-one pipeline stages and writes a per-stage log with stdout hashes; the last stage checks that every number printed in the manuscript and its tables is traceable to a file the pipeline writes, and exits non-zero if one is not. The deposit contains the analysis scripts, the preregistration record with its revision history, the derived per-point attributes for the 799 labelled points — lithological class and fault distance — the literature weight extraction, the figures, the audit log, and the anonymized manuscript and supplementary material that the last stage reads. The primary sources are not redistributed: the geological mapping and fault traces of the Hellenic Survey of Geology and Mineral Exploration are available under institutional access only. See README.md for each source and its access terms; MANIFEST.txt lists every deposited file with its md5. Changes since v1.1: the target journal is Environmental Impact Assessment Review rather than Omega; a twenty-first stage checks the provenance of every number in the submitted documents; the comparison of the two lithological codings is a stage rather than two runs sequenced by hand, after a clean pass was found to leave both codings’ outputs holding the same distribution; the Fisher’s exact test of the permeability contrast, previously computed outside the pipeline, is computed by the script that draws Figure S2; the figure scripts share figstyle.py, which embeds TrueType fonts and pins the font family, after two runs of the same pipeline produced figures in two different typefaces; fig2.py and fig3.py, which produce two of the submitted figures, were added to the audit, having been outside it; range_weights.py replaces a script that had been deleted; rapidfuzz is declared in requirements.txt after a silent fallback had changed the scheme count from 129 to 125; and make_deposit.py builds the archive from an explicit list instead of by hand.

items.summary: Analysis code and computed evidence store for the manuscript "An exact recurrence test for acquisition-chain bounds in vehicle telemetry: the closed ECU surface yields nothing, and the one detection lies in the logger we built ourselves", submitted to Sensors and Actuators A: Physical. This deposit contains code and derived results only. The underlying telemetry is published separately under its own DOIs, which fetch_data.py downloads and checksum-verifies before analysis, so the published figures are reproducible from the public record. Study design: observational audit of already-deposited telemetry (seven recording sessions). No experimental control, no intervention, no independent replication, and no statistical power for population-level inference. Headlines formulated after measurement rather than pre-declared in config.json are labelled exploratory in the manuscript. Multiplicity: this deposit is one of 15 analyses drawn from the same corpus of seven sessions, one vehicle and one rider. No correction for multiple comparisons is applied across that family, so the family-wise error rate is not controlled. Repository commit of record: 37f7b2147b26
items.title: Reproducibility package (I-21): An exact recurrence test for acquisition-chain bounds in vehicle telemetry: the closed ECU surface yields nothing, and the one detection lies in the logger we built ourselves

items.summary: Self-contained computational materials accompanying "Verifiable approval-release decisions for construction project management: A provenance-aware contract and automated evidence" by Ahmad Baghdadi. Version 4.0.0 includes source code, complete generated inputs and results, schemas, exact witnesses, a de-identified calendar encoding, benchmark records and SHA-256 checksums. This version adds 83 conventional priority-list levelling comparisons under identical constraints: 72 tied peaks and 11 one-gate improvements, with sufficient exact certificates for all 83. A complete two-plan PROV-O example passes the domain and provenance SHACL profiles and preserves every decision field after RDF exchange. The suite comprises 145 automated tests. Earlier computational evidence includes generated extraction, 360 controlled record comparisons, exact wave bounds, nine calendar scenarios and 80 saved benchmark plans with renewed arithmetic audit. S14 preparation includes blank independent-annotation and approval registers plus a precision/recall evaluator with explicit denominators. No native baseline or independent annotations are available; field validation has not been executed. Case A remains historical aggregates only. Calendar B is a prior encoding with assumed review windows. Supplementary Table S1 identifies the deposited components and the supplement consolidates the evidence limits.
items.title: Reproducibility materials for verifiable approval-release decisions in construction project management

items.summary: This record provides the public reproducibility materials associated with the study The Unequal Cultural City: Functional Differentiation and Spatial Inequality in London’s Cultural Infrastructure . The repository contains analytical code, public-safe derived neighbourhood data, spatial weights, source provenance, methodological protocols, confirmatory and robustness outputs, joint spatial re-estimation results, and supplementary materials for 4,994 Greater London 2021 LSOAs and a 2022 common-vintage cultural-infrastructure dataset. The study measures proximity-weighted availability of recorded cultural infrastructure and distinguishes Production from Encounter/Presentation functions. The two functions strongly overlap spatially. Their most consistently detected direct difference concerns metropolitan centrality: both decline with distance from London’s Central Activities Zone, with a steeper Encounter gradient. The differential deprivation association is model- and construct-sensitive, while the density difference remains unresolved. Cultural sustainability is treated as a bounded implication of the observed infrastructure configuration rather than as a directly measured sustainability outcome. The repository excludes raw site-level address/UPRN data and copyrighted source documents. Exact source provenance, reconstruction instructions, checksums, component-specific rights information, and reproducibility metadata are included.
items.title: Data, Code and Reproducibility Materials for "The Unequal Cultural City: Functional Differentiation and Spatial Inequality in London's Cultural Infrastructure"

items.summary: This record provides the public, non-confidential analytical and reproducibility materials supporting the manuscript “When Does Seismic–Geotechnical Data Fusion Add Value? A Borehole-Aware Empirical-to-Synthetic Validation Framework for Urban Tunnelling.” The study develops and audits a borehole-aware empirical-to-synthetic framework for evaluating whether adding downhole seismic information provides defensible incremental value in predicting the Ménard pressuremeter modulus under held-out validation. The empirical benchmark comprises 41 support-matched pressuremeter–seismic records across 21 independent boreholes from the Isfahan Metro Line 2 investigation. The framework compares a reference model, a geotechnical/geological-depth baseline, a seismic-only branch, naive multimodal fusion, and a dependence-aware fusion branch using leave-one-borehole-out validation. The public release contains a de-identified 41-record benchmark dataset, final manuscript Figure 1–5 assets, the current Supplementary Material and Supplementary Figure S1, released derived analytical outputs, provenance and reproducibility documentation, reproducibility and repository-audit scripts, computational-environment specifications, and SHA-256 integrity information. The de-identified dataset replaces source borehole identifiers with pseudonymous identifiers and excludes borehole coordinates and other spatially identifying source information. The underlying Isfahan Metro Line 2 geotechnical, geophysical, and pressuremeter source records are controlled by the Isfahan Urban Railway Organization and are not publicly redistributable. Original source workbooks, proprietary project documents, spatially identifying information, and other restricted source-derived materials are intentionally excluded from this public archive. Permission was obtained to use and publish the de-identified, non-confidential data extracted from the project report and the derived analytical information included in this release. The public code component provides scripts for reproducing the released manuscript-level benchmark metrics and verifying the integrity and consistency of the deposited files. These scripts do not contain the restricted original project records or proprietary source-data processing materials. The archive is intended to support transparent audit and reproducibility of the released derived analyses while preserving the access restrictions applying to the underlying project data.
items.title: When Does Seismic–Geotechnical Data Fusion Add Value? — Project 06 Data and Reproducibility Package

items.summary: Welcome to WARP WARP (WDL Analysis Research Pipelines) repository is a collection of cloud-optimized pipelines for processing biological data from the Broad Institute Data Sciences Platform and collaborators. The contents of this repository are open source and released under the BSD 3-Clause license . Table of Contents WARP Overview Navigating WARP Using WARP WARP Versioning and Releasing Testing in WARP Feedback Acknowledgements WARP Overview WARP pipelines provide robust, standardized data analysis for the Broad Institute Genomics Platform and large consortia like the Human Cell Atlas and the BRAIN Initiative. You can count on WARP for rigorously scientifically validated, high scale, reproducible and open source pipelines. Our pipelines are written as "workflows" using the Workflow Description Language (WDL) and they process a broad spectrum of "omic" and array-related datasets (see the overview table below). | Pipeline Category | Data Types | | --- | --- | | Germline Variant Discovery | Genomes, Exomes | | Genotyping Arrays | Variant discovery, Chip validation, Joint array analysis | | Single-cell/nuclei Transcriptomics | Droplet based (10x Genomics), Smartseq2 | | Single-cell Epigenomics | Single nuclei ATAC-seq, Single nuclei MethylC-seq | | Joint Genotyping | Genomes, Exomes | | Somatic Alignment (beta) | Exomes | Try our pipelines in Terra , a platform for collaborative cloud analysis! Learn how in the Using WARP section. Navigating WARP All versioned and released pipelines are in one of the three pipelines subdirectories: broad (pipelines for the Broad Institute's Genomics Platform), cemba (pipelines for the BRAIN Initiative) or skylab (pipelines for the Human Cell Atlas Project). Each pipeline directory hosts a main workflow WDL that includes a pipeline version number and a corresponding changelog file. Workflows may call additional WDLs, referred to as tasks, that are located in the tasks directory. Pipelines that are in progress or have not yet been validated are in the beta-pipelines folder. Using WARP There are three ways to use WARP pipelines: 1. Download the workflow and run on a WDL-compatible execution engine WDL workflows run on multiple systems, including Cromwell , miniWDL , and dxWDL (see the openwdl documentation ). To run a pipeline's latest release, first navigate to WARP Releases , search for your pipeline's tag, and download the pipeline's assets (the WDL workflow, the JSON, and the ZIP with accompanying dependencies; see Optimus example below). You can also access a pipeline's release page by selecting the pipeline version number at the top of the pipeline's README. After downloading the pipeline's assets, launch the workflow following your execution engine's instructions. 2. Run the pipeline in Terra Several WARP pipelines are available in public workspaces on the Terra cloud platform. These workspaces include both the WDL workflow and downsampled data so that you can test the pipeline at low-cost. If you are new to Terra, you can get started by registering with your Google account and visiting Terra Support . After registration, search for WARP-related workspaces with the "warp-pipelines" tag. To test the pipeline, clone (make a copy of) the workspace following the instructions in this Terra Support guide . 3. Run or export the pipeline from Dockstore Dockstore is a GA4GH compliant open platform for sharing Docker-based tools like WDL workflows. You can find WARP pipelines in Dockstore and run them on the Dockstore platform or export them to other platforms (including Terra). To view all available pipelines, just search "warp" in the Dockstore search and browse the workflow list. See Dockstore documentation for details on launching the workflow. items.summary: This reproducibility compendium accompanies the study “From Prediction Accuracy to Process Robustness: Condition-Aware Stability Frontiers for Ti-6Al-4V Laser Powder Bed Fusion.” The study performs a condition-aware secondary analysis of open Ti-6Al-4V laser powder bed fusion melt-pool data to evaluate productivity-stability trade-offs beyond conventional prediction accuracy. The analysis quantifies scan-velocity-dependent changes in melt-pool width and variability, identifies Pareto-optimal operating conditions, derives epsilon-constrained process windows, models orientation anisotropy using a twofold circular harmonic formulation, and recomputes published row-random classifier metrics from the reported confusion matrix. The archive contains the condition-level source statistics used in the analysis, derived CSV outputs, Python analysis and figure-generation scripts, publication-ready figures, environment specifications, automated verification scripts, provenance metadata, a data dictionary, manuscript-to-result mappings, licensing information, and SHA-256 checksums. The package does not reconstruct synthetic individual-level observations from the underlying high-resolution dataset. All inferential results are based on reported process-condition summaries, consistent with the manuscript's condition-aware analytical framework.
items.title: "From Prediction Accuracy to Process Robustness: Condition-Aware Stability Frontiers for Ti-6Al-4V Laser Powder Bed Fusion."

items.summary: v1.0.0 — Initial Audited Analysis Code Release Initial public release of the audited analysis code supporting: Cross-Cohort Transportability, Calibration, and Incremental Value of Breast DCE-MRI Radiomics for Predicting Pathologic Complete Response Included Preprocessing and cohort preparation scripts DCE-MRI radiomics extraction workflow Clinical, radiomics, and combined modeling pipelines Internal and external validation scripts Bootstrap comparison analyses Figure-generation scripts Reproducibility and analysis-workflow documentation Version-pinned Python environment Reproducibility scope This release contains the audited analysis code and documentation used for the reported analyses. No patient-level data, medical images, masks, prediction files, or derived radiomics matrices are distributed in this repository. Three historical provenance gaps are explicitly documented in the repository and should be considered when interpreting end-to-end reproducibility. Data The analyses use publicly available breast DCE-MRI resources. Dataset access information and applicable licensing are documented in docs/DATA_AVAILABILITY.md . License Code in this repository is released under the MIT License. Dataset licenses remain governed by their respective data providers. Release: v1.0.0 Release date: 2026-10-08
